power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: As in the SNT protocol, each participant received 50 iTBS sessions (1,800 pulses; 10 sessions/day over 5 days) delivered using a neuronavigated TMS system. As in SNT, stimulation intensity was linearly adjusted for the cortical depth of the target relative to the motor hotspot (Stokes et al., 2005). We additionally used post hoc electric field modeling to characterize the network composition and baseline sACC connectivity of TAO-TMS hotspots, using BeamF3 as a conventional anatomical reference. We also assessed pre-treatment to post-treatment functional connectivity (FC) changes, and performed an exploratory health economic comparison with ECT. This proof-of-concept study evaluated the feasibility, tolerability as measured by treatment completion, preliminary clinical outcomes, and targeting characteristics of TAO-TMS in a naturalistic TRD population with complex psychiatric comorbidities. Given the pilot design, the institutional review board (IRB) application included an approximate G*Power calculation indicating a minimum of 20 participants with paired pre-post observations, based on a large within-participant effect (Cohen's d = 0.8; paired-sample t-test; α = 0.05). Under these assumptions, this sample size provides approximately 92.4% power to detect the assumed effect using a paired two-tailed t-test. Twenty-one participants were enrolled; one withdrew during treatment, leaving 20 participants with immediate post-treatment data.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. Participants were asked at the end of each treatment session whether they had experienced any side effects or discomfort.
Participants were assessed at baseline, post-treatment, 1-month and 3-month follow-ups using the MADRS score (Montgomery and Åsberg, 1979) 1993).
Participants completed a second MRI session on average 5.0 ± 1.9 days after treatment, consisting of one T1-weighted structural scan and two restingstate fMRI runs.
Of 27 participants screened, 21 participants were recruited (mean age 35.1 ± 12.3 years; 57% female; 81% Chinese, 19% South Asian).
The enrolled participants had 4.7 ± 2.3 failed antidepressant trials, and 19% had previously received electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).
The average number of comorbid psychiatric diagnoses was 1.6, and only three participants had no comorbid psychiatric diagnosis.
Four representative participants are shown here, with targets (green circles) displayed on native pial surfaces (top) and native T1 images (bottom).
FC changes for the remaining participants are shown in Figures S6 and S7.
Written informed consent was obtained from participants (or their parent/legal guardian/next of kin) to participate in the study.
However, Zhao et al. excluded participants with any secondary psychiatric disorder or prior ECT, whereas our participants averaged 1.7 psychiatric comorbidities and 19% had previously received ECT.
Although 38% of our participants had previously received scalp-based TMS, ECT populations may include a greater proportion of patients referred after TMS nonresponse.
During the 10-minute rs-fMRI scans, participants were instructed to keep their eyes open, maintain fixation on a central cross, let their minds wander naturally, and avoid repetitive thoughts.

Participants completed a second MRI session on average 5.0 ± 1.9 days after treatment, consisting of one T1-weighted structural scan and two resting-state fMRI runs acquired using the same imaging protocol. fMRI preprocessing T1-weighted MRI data was processed using FreeSurfer (Fischl, 2012).

text.text: Personalized connectivity-guided accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) has shown promising efficacy for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in carefully selected trial populations.
Evidence remains limited in naturalistic TRD patients with complex psychiatric comorbidities often excluded from such trials.

Here, we report an open-label, single-arm proofof-concept study of a personalized connectivity-guided targeting approach, TAO-TMS (Treebased Algorithm for Optimized Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation), in a naturalistic Asian TRD sample.
Participants averaged 1.7 psychiatric comorbidities, including personality disorders, autism and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Of 21 enrolled participants, 20 completed 50 iTBS sessions over 5 days.
The primary outcome was response rate (≥50% reduction in Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale score) immediately after treatment.
Among participants with available data, response rates were 65% immediately after treatment, 50% at 1 month and 31% at 3 months.
In exploratory analyses, 70% responded within 4 weeks post-treatment; the corresponding rate was 83% in a subgroup of participants meeting typical randomized-trial eligibility criteria (N = 12).
For descriptive local context, we note that a retrospective cohort at the same hospital receiving non-accelerated TMS with scalp-based BeamF3 targeting had an immediate response rate of 22%.
Post hoc electric-field modeling confirmed that TAO-TMS achieved the intended targeting of attention networks.
Statistically significant functional connectivity changes were observed in each participant, but varied widely across participants.
Exploratory economic modeling suggested lower one-year costs for TAO-TMS than electroconvulsive therapy, with similar quality-adjusted life-years.
TAO-TMS was feasible and well tolerated.

Its preliminary clinical signal warrants evaluation in randomized controlled trials. v2024.04.1 (Posit Software, PBC, Boston, MA), with modeling conducted in TreeAge Pro 2023 356 R² (TreeAge Software, LLC, Williamstown, MA).

Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) is defined as major depressive disorder (MDD) that fails to respond to adequate trials of at least two antidepressant medications (Thase and Rush, 1997; Conway et al., 2017; Tor et al., 2022). 30% of patients with MDD are estimated to be treatment-resistant (Rush et al., 2006; McIntyre et al., 2023).

We also assessed pre-treatment to post-treatment functional connectivity (FC) changes, and performed an exploratory health economic comparison with ECT.

This proof-of-concept study evaluated the feasibility, tolerability as measured by treatment completion, preliminary clinical outcomes, and targeting characteristics of TAO-TMS in a naturalistic TRD population with complex psychiatric comorbidities.

Given the pilot design, the institutional review board (IRB) application included an approximate G*Power calculation indicating a minimum of 20 participants with paired pre-post observations, based on a large within-participant effect (Cohen's d = 0.8; paired-sample t-test; α = 0.05).
Under these assumptions, this sample size provides approximately 92.4% power to detect the assumed effect using a paired two-tailed t-test.
Twenty-one participants were enrolled; one withdrew during treatment, leaving 20 participants with immediate post-treatment data.
Because the calculation was based on continuous pre-post change rather than the binary primary response endpoint, it did not constitute a formal power calculation for the primary endpoint.
The study was not powered for the subgroup, neuroimaging, or health-economic analyses.
Stimulation was delivered with a MagPro X100 stimulator (MagVenture, Farum, Denmark).

To ensure precise and reproducible coil placement, we utilized the Axilum Robotics TMS-Cobot (Axilum Robotics, Strasbourg, France) with the Localite neuronavigation system (Localite GmbH, Sankt Augustin, Germany).
Real-time neuronavigation was maintained to keep the coil within 2 mm of the personalized target.
We employed the Stanford Accelerated Intelligent Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT) stimulation protocol using our TAO-TMS targets.
Each session delivered 1800 pulses consisting of bursts of 3 pulses at 50 Hz, repeated at 5 Hz, with a train duration of 2 seconds and an intertrain interval of 8 seconds.
The coil (MagVenture Cool-B65) was positioned tangential to the scalp with the handle oriented at 45 degrees to the mid-sagittal line.
Participants received 10 6 sessions per day over 5 consecutive days (50 sessions total).
Sessions were separated by a 50minute inter-session interval.
Stimulation was delivered at 90% resting motor threshold (RMT), linearly adjusted for the cortical depth of the target relative to the motor hotspot (Stokes et al., 2005; Cole et al., 2020).

The Localite neuronavigation system recorded the coil position for each delivered pulse relative to the participant's native MRI.

These records were used to derive the actual treatment location for each pulse, and the Euclidean distance between this location and the intended TAO-TMS target was calculated in the individual's native T1 space.
Distances were averaged across all delivered pulses within a treatment session to obtain the mean spatial deviation ("COBOT accuracy") for each participant.

text.text: To explore whether coil orientation and targeting constraints were associated with clinical improvement, we conducted two sets of exploratory analyses.
First, the coil orientation in our trial was fixed at 45 degrees, following the SNT stimulation protocol.
For each participant, we modeled alternative coil orientations to minimize hotspot sACC FC (i.e., maximize anticorrelations).
The difference between the minimum hotspot sACC FC and the actual hotspot sACC FC (based on the 45-degree coil angle) was then correlated with percentage MADRS improvement across participants.
A positive correlation would suggest that optimizing coil orientation to further minimize hotspot sACC FC might potentially improve clinical outcomes.
We repeated the same analysis by replacing hotspot sACC FC with attentional-network 10 engagement.
Here, a negative correlation would suggest that optimizing coil orientation to further maximize attention-network engagement might potentially improve clinical outcomes.
Second, recall that TAO-TMS restricted the target to be near the scalp and to be within the attention networks.

To explore the impact of these targeting constraints, personalized TMS targets were regenerated without the near-scalp constraint, and the Euclidean distance between these unconstrained targets and the original targets was correlated with percentage MADRS improvement.
A negative correlation would suggest that the near-scalp constraint was potentially worsening clinical outcomes.
The same analysis was repeated by removing both the near-scalp and attentional network constraints.

We conducted an exploratory cost-effectiveness analysis comparing TAO-TMS with ECT using a standard hybrid decision tree-Markov model over a one-year time horizon (Figure S1; Sonnenberg and Beck, 1993).

text.text: Analyses were performed from healthcare system and societal perspectives.
The model comprised two stages with the same structure for TAO-TMS and ECT.

First, the decision tree classified patients immediately after treatment into one of three acute-outcome categories: responders (≥50% reduction in MADRS), partial responders (≥25% but <50% reduction in MADRS), or nonresponders (<25% reduction in MADRS).

text.text: Second, at 1 month after treatment, the same patients entered the Markov model and were assigned to one of three health states based on their MADRS score at that assessment: remission (MADRS <11), partial relapse (MADRS 11-20), or relapse (MADRS >20).
text.formatted: Second, at 1 month after treatment, the same patients entered the Markov model and were assigned to one of three health states based on their MADRS score at that assessment: remission (MADRS <11), partial relapse (MADRS 11-20), or relapse (MADRS >20).

text.text: Thus, the acute-outcome categories described the initial percentage improvement, whereas the Markov health states described symptom severity at 1 month.
During each subsequent monthly cycle through month 12, patients could remain in their current health state or transition to another state.
Treatment-specific probabilities were assigned to this common model structure.

For TAO-TMS, data from the present trial were used to determine both the probabilities of the acuteoutcome categories and the probabilities of moving from each acute-outcome category immediately after treatment to each health state at 1 month after treatment (when the Markov model began).
Subsequent transition probabilities among the health states were estimated from changes observed between the 1-month and 3-month assessments.
Because these assessments 11 were separated by two months, the observed transition probabilities were converted into monthly probabilities assuming constant transition hazards.
These monthly probabilities were then applied through month 12.
For ECT, the corresponding acute-outcome and follow-up probabilities were obtained from published economic evaluations of nonpsychotic TRD populations (Zhao et al., 2018; Fitzgibbon et al., 2020).

text.text: Thus, the decision tree characterized percentage improvement immediately after treatment, whereas the Markov states characterized absolute symptom severity during follow-up.
The Markov model used monthly cycles through month 12.
During each cycle, patients could remain in their current health state or transition to another state.
Treatment-specific probabilities were assigned to this common model structure.

For TAO-TMS, data from the present trial determined the probabilities of the acute-outcome categories and the probabilities of moving from each acute-outcome category immediately after treatment to each Markov health state at 1 month after treatment.
Subsequent transition probabilities among the health states were estimated using changes observed between the 1-month and 3-month assessments.
Analyses used patients with the observations required to estimate each probability; missing outcomes were not imputed.
Because the 1-month and 3month assessments were separated by two months, the observed two-month transition probabilities were converted into monthly probabilities.
The resulting monthly probabilities were applied through month 12.
This extrapolation assumes that transition probabilities observed between months 1 and 3 remained constant during subsequent follow-up.

Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥ 21; (2) DSM-5 diagnosis of MDD with current major depressive episode; (3) baseline MADRS ≥ 20; and (4) at least one failed antidepressant trial.

Exclusion criteria included psychosis, recent substance abuse, acute suicidality requiring inpatient care, significant neurological disorders (e.g. epilepsy), pregnancy, or contraindications to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).
Participants maintained stable medications during the treatment week.

Two descriptive metrics were calculated.
First, network engagement was defined as the percentage of the E-field hotspot surface area falling within each of the 17 individualized cortical networks.
Second, baseline hotspot sACC FC was calculated by correlating the sACC time course with an E-field-weighted average of DLPFC vertex time courses (Elbau et al., 2023).
More negative values indicate stronger sACC anticorrelation and may indicate better target quality (Weigand et al., 2018; Elbau et al., 2023).

However, because TAO-TMS was designed around both characteristics whereas BeamF3 was not, their comparison characterized modeled network engagement rather than establishing superior target quality or clinical efficacy.

E-field characteristics (network specificity and hotspot sACC FC) of TAO-TMS and BeamF3 targets were compared based on the 20 participants who completed all 50 TMS sessions with paired two-tailed t-tests.
Treatment-related functional connectivity changes were examined in 18 participants who completed a post-treatment scan with acceptable head motion.

Within-participant whole-brain FC change between baseline and post-treatment was quantified using xDF (Afyouni et al., 2019), which accounts for temporal autocorrelation in fMRI time series and yields an edge-wise zstatistic for FC change (post-treatment minus baseline) in each individual.

Psychiatric complexity may have contributed to our observed clinical outcomes.

In accelerated iTBS trials using anatomical/scalp targets, naturalistic cohorts with substantial psychiatric comorbidity have reported response rates of 22%-28% (Ye et al., 2024; Goodman et al., 2025; Persson et al., 2025), compared with 52%-75% in studies applying more restrictive psychiatric eligibility criteria (Luehr et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Ramos et al., 2025).
Although confounded by population and protocol differences, these informal cross-study comparisons suggest that psychiatric complexity may influence treatment response.
Stronger evidence comes from within-study comparisons of patients with and without complex comorbidities.
Hearne et al. (2025) reported response rates of 74% in trial-eligible patients and 44% in patients with complex comorbidities following unaccelerated connectivityguided iTBS.
Consistently, when we excluded participants with autism, OCD and personality disorders from our TAO-TMS sample, the response rate in the remaining subgroup (N = 12)
Zhao et al. (2024) provides an informative comparison: the study's iTBS arm delivered the same 90,000-pulse, five-day schedule using a predefined group-average left DLPFC target.
Response rates were comparable with our study, but acute symptom reduction and remission were numerically higher in our study.
However, Zhao et al. excluded participants with any secondary psychiatric disorder or prior ECT, whereas our participants averaged 1.7 psychiatric comorbidities and 19% had previously received ECT.

The similar response rates could indicate no clinical advantage of individualized TAO-TMS targeting over Zhao's group-average target or reflect differences in psychiatric complexity and prior treatment exposure.
These explanations cannot be separated through cross-study comparison.
Targeting may also influence outcomes.
Two recent randomized trials directly compared individualized connectivity-guided targeting with conventional scalp-based targeting for accelerated iTBS.
Taylor et al. (2026a) found superior outcomes with individualized connectivity-guided targeting at one month, while Li et al. (2026) reported an advantage at week 6.

However, Li et al. (2026) excluded participants with any secondary psychiatric disorder, while Taylor et al. (2026a) applied eligibility criteria similar to those of the SNT trials, which excluded several psychiatric comorbidities represented in our sample.
These restrictive criteria leave uncertainty about the generalizability of their findings to more complex, naturalistic populations.

Separately, Taylor et al. (2026b) found similar improvement in depressive symptoms following et al. (2022) averaged approximately 0.43 psychiatric comorbidities per participant, compared with 1.7 in our sample.
More recently, Feyder et al. (2026) reported SNT outcomes with the same 5-day stimulation schedule in a larger, naturalistic multi-center sample.
Although participants in Feyder et al. averaged approximately 1.0 psychiatric comorbidity versus 1.7 in our sample, acute MADRS reduction was 41.3% versus 57% in our study.
These cross-study findings cannot establish relative effectiveness.

A larger sample size would be necessary to identify reproducible treatment-related FC changes and relate them to baseline psychiatric heterogeneity and clinical response.30Health economics: policy and system-level implications Under the base-case assumptions, exploratory health economic modeling estimated that TAO-TMS was less costly than ECT by approximately US$8,214 per patient from the healthcare system perspective and US$14,894 from the societal perspective, while QALYs were similar.
TAO-TMS remained less costly, with similar QALYs, across shorter time horizons (3 and 6 months) and in the conservative two-state Markov model.
In one-way sensitivity analyses, the modeled cost of ECT was the most influential parameter: TAO-TMS lost dominance when the ECT treatment cost fell below US$539.
Probabilistic simulations estimated a >85% probability that TAO-TMS was cost-effective at willingness-to-pay thresholds aligned with Singapore gross domestic product (GDP) per capita.

Because ECT eligibility was not assessed, we cannot determine whether all TAO-TMS participants would have been ECT candidates.
The analysis therefore combined outcomes from this single-arm study with literature-derived ECT parameters from nonpsychotic TRD populations.
Although 38% of our participants had previously received scalp-based TMS, ECT populations may include a greater proportion of patients referred after TMS nonresponse.

These analyses were limited by our small sample size, and larger randomized studies are needed to determine whether integrating E-field modeling improves targeting or clinical outcomes.

Conclusions This open-label, single-arm proof-of-concept study supports the feasibility and tolerability of connectivity-guided accelerated iTBS in a naturalistic Asian TRD population that included psychiatric comorbidities commonly excluded from previous accelerated iTBS trials.

Each participant underwent a T1-weighted structural scan and two 10-minute resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) runs prior to treatment.
The structural data were obtained with a T1w MPRAGE sequence using the following acquisition parameters: TR = 2200 ms; TE = 2.45 ms; FOV = 256 × 232 mm; voxel size = 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 mm.

During the 10-minute rs-fMRI scans, participants were instructed to keep their eyes open, maintain fixation on a central cross, let their minds wander naturally, and avoid repetitive thoughts.
The scalp-based BeamF3 (Beam et al., 2009) stimulation location was also identified and marked on the scalp using a vitamin E capsule.
